# Purpose

The purpose of this guide is to help you prepare for the Reproducible Research with Quarto and GitHub course by:

1. [setting up the required software](#software) on your computer,
2. [choosing a project of your own](#project) to work on during the course, and
3. optionally, [printing two documents](#printing) to use during the course.

Following these preparation steps will allow you to fully participate in all course activities without technical interruptions. The time you invest in preparation will make the sessions more productive and easier to follow.

If you encounter any issues during the pre-course setup, or if you have any related questions, please don't hesitate to get in touch with me via email at [resul.umit@durham.ac.uk](mailto:resul.umit@durham.ac.uk).

# 1. Setting up the required software {#software}

You might already have some of the software that we need --- R, RStudio, Quarto, LaTeX, Git, and R packages --- installed on your computer. However, to ensure we are all working with the same setup, please check for updates or simply install the latest versions. Installing fresh copies will ensure compatibility and prevent any version-related issues.

## 1.1 Install R and RStudio

R is a powerful, open-source programming language. RStudio is a free integrated development environment (IDE) for R, which we will use throughout the course to work with R, Quarto, Git, and GitHub.

-   For installation on a **Windows** machine, you can [download R here](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/), and [RStudio here](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/download.html).
-   For installation on a **Mac** machine, you can [download R here](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/), and [RStudio here](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/download.html). Note that you should download the correct version of R for your Mac, depending on whether it has an Apple (M) or an Intel processor.

If you already have RStudio, you can check whether it needs updating: in RStudio, go to `Help -> Check for RStudio Updates`.

## 1.2 Check Quarto

Quarto is the publishing system at the centre of this course. It comes bundled with RStudio, so there is nothing to install separately if your RStudio is up to date. Note that updating R does not update Quarto --- updating RStudio does.

To check your Quarto version, start RStudio, open the `Terminal` tab next to the `Console`[^terminal], type the following, and press `Enter`:

[^terminal]: If you do not see a `Terminal` tab, open one: in RStudio, go to `Tools -> Terminal -> New Terminal`.

```{.bash}
quarto --version
```

If the number shown is lower than 1.7, please install the latest version of Quarto separately, from [quarto.org/docs/get-started](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/). RStudio will then use this newer version.

## 1.3 Install TinyTeX

To create PDF documents, Quarto needs a LaTeX distribution. TinyTeX is a lightweight distribution designed for this purpose. To install it, type the following in the `Terminal` tab in RStudio, and press `Enter`:

```{.bash}
quarto install tinytex
```

You may skip this step if you already have a LaTeX distribution, such as MiKTeX or MacTeX, but then, please make sure they are up to date as well.

## 1.4 Install Git and create a GitHub account

Git is a free software that keeps track of the versions of your files, on your computer. GitHub is a website that keeps a copy of these versions online, and allows for collaboration. We will use both through RStudio.

-   On a **Windows** machine, install 'Git for Windows', [downloading it here](https://gitforwindows.org), and accept the default settings.
-   On a **Mac** machine, type `git --version` in the `Terminal` tab in RStudio. If Git is missing, macOS will offer to install it, as part of its command line developer tools. Alternatively, you can [download Git here](https://git-scm.com/downloads).

Then, sign up for a free account at [github.com](https://github.com). Note that usernames are public: either choose an anonymous username (e.g., `asdf029348`), or choose one carefully, as it may become a part of your online presence.

## 1.5 Install R packages

In this course, we will be using functions from the following packages: `quarto`, `dplyr`, `ggplot2`, `modelsummary`, `usethis`, and `gitcreds`.

Please install these now --- copy and paste the following code into the `Console` and press `Enter` on your keyboard to run it.

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("quarto", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "modelsummary",
                   "usethis", "gitcreds"))
```

Wait until the installation finishes. You will know it's finished when the `Console` prompt (`>`) reappears and no further output is printed.

## 1.6 Test your setup

Finally, check that everything works together, using the test file, `the_test.qmd`, attached to the email with which you received this guide:

1. save `the_test.qmd` in a folder on your computer, such as your `Documents` folder,
2. open it in RStudio, following `File -> Open File`, and
3. click the `Render` button, above the document.

The first rendering may take a few minutes, as TinyTeX downloads the LaTeX packages that it needs. Please make sure that you are connected to the internet, and be patient.

If everything works, a new file, `the_test.pdf`, will appear in the same folder, with a congratulatory message and a summary of your setup. If any item in this summary is in bold, please follow the instruction next to it.

If the rendering fails, please read the error message. If it names a package that is missing, install that package as shown above. Otherwise, make sure that you have completed all of the steps above, restart RStudio, and try again --- or get in touch with me.

# 2. Choosing a project of your own {#project}

In between the two days of the course, you will start converting one of your own projects into Quarto, and continue working on it throughout the course, with my help. Please choose one such project in advance, preferably

- one that you can convert freely, e.g., single-authored, or with co-authors who are happy for you to try Quarto,
- one with tables or figures based on data, and
- one that you are working on, or have worked on.

This could be part of your dissertation, a seminar paper, or a separate project that you are personally or professionally interested in.

Please have the files that belong to this project ready on your computer, such as

- the text, in whatever format you are writing it now (e.g., Word),
- the data and any R scripts, and
- your references, exported as a `.bib` file from your reference manager (e.g., Zotero).

# 3. Optional: Printing two documents {#printing}

This step is entirely optional --- if you prefer not to print anything, that is perfectly fine.

During the course, you will work in RStudio while following the slides and reading a PDF document. If you are working on a single, small screen, such as a laptop, having some of these on paper can save screen space. If you wish, print the following and keep them at hand:

- `reproduce_this.pdf`, attached to the email with which you received this guide: the document that we will re-create during the course (11 pages)
- the [Quarto cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/quarto.pdf), which summarises much of what we will cover (2 pages)

Both documents will also be available electronically during the course.
